author: Staff Writer
title: Creating sculptures helps relieve artist's grief - NewsBreak
text:
By Staff Writer ,
1 hours ago
VENICE — It was a devastating day when Ginny DeGreef lost her husband three years ago, two months before their 41st anniversary. Moving past her deepest grief, she found her way back to a previous love — the art of sculpture.
“My passion for sculpting began when I was in my 20s,” she said. “I still have some of those pieces, but due to an upward career move and life changes, I gave it up.”
She renewed her passion for sculpting now in her 70s and began taking classes with Beth Burgan at Venice Art Center in Venice.
Burgan is a trained sculptor who teaches sculpting classes and sells her own works at VAC.
Sculpting classes have a long history at VAC. Mary Moscatelli, CEO, said sculpting has been a popular class at VAC since long before her arrival 17 years ago. The art center dates back to the 1950s.
“Sculpting is part of the 500 classes held here for adults and children,” Moscatelli said.
Since starting classes at VAC two years ago, DeGreef has created a half dozen pieces of sculpture and is passionate about the process. She is pleased that Burgan guides her work and leaves her alone to work out figures, hallowing out and pinning a piece, and adding the finishing touches. She is grateful for the kiln.
“I don’t think of anything else when I’m sculpting. I think it is something to help me with my grief. My husband was my everything. He also left behind our two daughters and three granddaughters.”
DeGreef, of Venice for the past nine years, is originally from Warwickshire, England, 20 minutes from Shakespere’s home at Stratford On Avon.
She followed her sister, Susan, to the United States in the 1960s, both taking work as an Au Pair for different families in New Jersey under a one-year contract. She then moved to Manhattan in the early 1970s near her brother.
Later she met Jean Pierre DeGreef, who was livng in Belgium. They were both single parents of girls — her daughter Lorna, his daughter Anouk. They married and lived in New York and New Jersey and eventually moved to Venice.
More of DeGreef’s artistic journey is in this Q&A.
When did you first become interested in creating art?
I drew and painted some as a kid. At about age 11 or 12, I was the art teacher’s pet. I learned a lot about art history and art appreciation. After seeing a copy of Michelangelo’s painting of God reaching toward Adam in the British Museum, I drew it as a child. I recently sculptured it.
I most likely inherited my creative genes from my father. He had wanted to go to art school but joined the military when World War II broke out. He eventually built a beautiful fireplace with Cotswold stone. He showed his creativity in the work that he did.
Did you take art classes and study sculptng before moving to Florida?
I studied sculpting in Manhattan years ago. I found satisfaction in sculpting that I never found with painting. There is something about building a sculpture that has more meaning.
What inspires your art?
The human form is inspiring. In New York, students modeled for us. Some work was three dimensional. A teacher inspired my sculpting.
I love working with clay. You can get into it by using the instruments used for clay. It differs from sculpting in wood, which is more abstract. Wood can have fissures which changes the dimensions.
How do you begin a piece?
Sometimes I have a vision. Other times, someone asks me to make something for them, like my granddaughter who asked me to make her a sculpture of a hand. I will do this.
Sometimes, I give pieces away. I gave a sculpture of Jesus’s face to a friend in Brussels because she said she loved it.
Do you perform all your sculpting at VAC’s studio?
My sculpting is done at the Art Center studio but I sometimes finish the piece on my lanai after using the kiln and drying it. That is when more creating and painting come to the forefront.
I want my work to look like the sculptures of old. People like modern things, like my guitarist, named “The Blues.” But I’m more old school. Florence, Italy, is where the David sculpture is. I love the classic artwork of these types of pieces. The medium is consistent.
I like casting in bronze but it is very expensive. I put my guitarist piece on wood, which is a more organic base and befitting for a guitarist. I’ll put “The Dancers, ” a male and female, on a marble base.
Have you won any awards or honors?
I won a Merit Award at VAC for my guitarist sculpture. I showed it at a reception at VAC and won a “People’s Choice” award.
I was honored by Suncoast Writers Guild. As a Guild member, I was able to be one of four artists to share a creative work at the Wm. H. Jervey Jr. Venice Library. I spoke about my two Indian heads sculpture — a male and female — titled ‘”Blue Turtle,” the title depicts the male. I created it when I was in my 20s.
My Indian heads piece was selected. It went to a writer for a short story, a poet created a poem, a Musicale musician performed music for it, and I spoke about it.
SWG’s vision is to fuse local artists, working in fusion with writers, poets, musicians, artists. At SWG events, the four artists build upon each other’s works: the poet writes a poem, the writer writes about the piece, a singer sings about the piece and the painter/sculptor speaks about it. It brings the creative world together.
How important is art in the world?
I believe art is most important. It gives beauty to the world. When you look at it, it takes you away. Fusing the arts keeps the world together. The arts are universal. We are all connected and we need to see more beauty in the world.
Your goal is to have your own show. When do you think that could happen?
I only started two years ago here and need more pieces to have my own show. I want to become known and earn enough trust for someone to ask: “Sculpt me.” But building that many pieces is life-consuming; I need to do more sculpting.
What are some of the challenges of sculpting?
Sculpting is hard work. For the dancers, I had to hollow out some of the clay, and what couldn’t be hollowed out I put pins through the form so the piece would not explode in the kiln. A sculpture that is too thick can break in the kiln, where it bakes for 24 hours. Then you can dry and paint it. After the kiln, you can either plug the pin holes with stoneware clay or paint.
